https://baltic-review.com/warsaw-festiva.text: Share Tweet 0 Warsaw’s relationship with food is moving into the centre of an urban conversation. The 18th edition of the Warsaw Under Construction festival opens on Sunday, 30 August, with a programme devoted to food sovereignty, local agriculture and the links between the capital and the surrounding Mazovian countryside. Organised by the Museum of Modern Art in Warsaw, the festival will run until 27 September. Rather than presenting food only as a matter of consumption, it treats farming, distribution, markets and everyday meals as elements of urban planning and civic life. The programme combines exhibitions, discussions, guided visits, workshops, walks, river trips and community events across Warsaw and the wider region. ([muzea.waw.pl](https://muzea.waw.pl/en/museums/modern-art-museum/exhibitions/warszawa-w-budowie-18-suwerenna-i-najedzona/?utm_source=openai)) A harvest gathering outside the museum The opening event will take place from 2 p.m. to 7 p.m. at the MOST Cooperative Farm on Gwintowa Street in the Siekierki area. Admission is free. Visitors will be able to tour the farm, meet the community involved in its upkeep and share refreshments prepared from this year’s harvest. The opening will also include two site-specific art projects. Artist Jan Sajdak will present a sculptural group titled Blades of Grass , while artist Gosia Kępa will introduce a land-art installation called Soil Profile and lead a workshop on making soil profiles. The afternoon will close with a performance by Urzeczeni, a musical project connected with the traditional culture of the Urzecze area south of Warsaw. ([artmuseum.pl](https://artmuseum.pl/en/events/warsaw-under-construction-18th-harvest-festival-at-the-cooperative-farm-in-most?utm_source=openai)) The choice of a working cooperative farm as the festival’s starting point is deliberate. It places cultivation, soil and seasonal production in the foreground, before the programme moves into museums, markets, shops, orchards and wholesale distribution sites. In this format, the city is presented not as an isolated consumer centre but as part of a larger food landscape. From the Vistula valley to the city market One of the festival’s recurring themes is the historical connection between Warsaw and the agricultural areas around it. The organisers point to the Urzecze microregion, whose villages and riverine landscapes have supplied the capital with vegetables, fruit, honey, dairy products and fish for generations. The programme will take visitors to several places that form part of the capital’s present-day food map, including orchards in Żoliborz, the Egipska market in Saska Kępa, the Zbiory food shop in Mokotów and the Bronisze wholesale market west of Warsaw. Other events will focus on the relationship between food, labour, technology and cooperative organisation. For residents, the festival offers a practical way to look at questions that can otherwise remain abstract. Where does food sold in the city come from? Which parts of the supply chain are visible to consumers, and which remain hidden? What role can small farms, neighbourhood shops and cooperatives play alongside large-scale distribution? Food as an urban-planning issue The organisers describe food sovereignty as an increasingly important element of contemporary city strategies. The concept does not imply that Warsaw could produce everything it consumes. Instead, it draws attention to the resilience of local networks, the preservation of agricultural land and the capacity of communities to understand and strengthen the systems on which daily life depends. This approach gives the festival an environmental dimension without reducing the subject to climate messaging. Soil, water, biodiversity, land use and transport all influence how food reaches the city. At the same time, local food systems are connected to culture: recipes, seasonal rituals, forms of work and relationships between urban residents and rural producers. Polish Radio’s coverage of the festival described the opening harvest gathering as a reminder of the long relationship between Warsaw, the river, the land and the people who work it. The station also highlighted the festival’s decision to move beyond a single exhibition space and use the city and Mazovia as its wider setting. ([polskieradio.pl](https://www.polskieradio.pl/podcasty/folkowy-poranek-dwojki/18-festiwal-warszawa-w-budowie-i-podroz-na-urzecze?utm_source=openai)) A month of public exploration After the opening, the programme will continue with public discussions, walks, visits and workshops. A 3 September conversation at the museum will examine how Warsaw might combine local resources, agricultural infrastructure, older forms of organisation and contemporary technologies when thinking about its food future. Later events will look at cooperatives, local shops and the role of food distribution in building more resilient cities. The festival’s strength lies in its constructive scale. It does not present a single solution or claim that local production can replace every wider supply chain. Instead, it invites residents to examine the food system as a shared civic environment: something shaped by farms, markets, roads, kitchens, institutions and consumer choices. By opening with a harvest celebration at an operating urban farm, Warsaw Under Construction 18 makes that argument tangible. For one month, food becomes a way to read the capital’s geography, its social relationships and its remaining connections to the cultivated landscapes beyond the city. https://www.worthynews.com/117474-hungar.text: Worthy Christian News > World News > Hungary’s Child Protection System Near Collapse As Government Report Reveals Abuse (Worthy News Investigation) Hungary’s Child Protection System Near Collapse As Government Report Reveals Abuse (Worthy News Investigation) Sunday, September 13, 2026 | Tag Cloud | Learn about our FREE SYNDICATION Service | Get the Worthy Brief by email! | Printer Friendly by Stefan J. Bos , Worthy News Europe Bureau Chief BUDAPEST, HUNGARY ( Worthy News ) – Hungary’s child protection system is on the verge of “structural collapse” as state investigators uncovered hunger, life-threatening buildings, severe neglect, and physical and sexual abuse impacting thousands of vulnerable children, according to an internal government report reviewed by Worthy News. The roughly 220-page assessment paints a devastating picture of serious failures that remained largely hidden from the public under the previous government of then-Prime Minister Viktor Orbán. Investigators described a system struggling with severe staff shortages, overcrowded facilities, inadequate mental-health care, and thousands of children who cannot be placed in appropriate homes. Government officials said earlier reports showed that senior authorities under Orbán had known about the problems for years but failed to act effectively. Separate inspection reports from 2024 detailing appalling conditions were not publicly released and investigative journalists eventually obtained them through litigation. Social media may not always show you what matters. Get Worthy News directly in your inbox. Hungary has about 23,000 children and young people in state care, while roughly 130,000 of the country’s more than 1.6 million children are officially considered at risk. Government data show thousands of child-abuse cases were recorded in state-run child protection institutions during 2024 and 2025, while 2,249 police reports were filed over the two years. SEXUAL ABUSE AND HUNGER In Budapest alone, 252 cases of child abuse were registered in 2023 and 2024, including physical and sexual violence. Elsewhere in Bács-Kiskun County in southern Hungary, a police investigation found that children at a special children’s home had submitted to sexual abuse by other youngsters in exchange for food. Investigators said no food—not even bread, butter, or jam—was available after the central kitchen closed at 6:30 p.m. local time. In Vas County in western Hungary, inspectors reported an increase in sexual abuse among children compared with the previous year, with the youngest perpetrator just nine years old. The assessment also describes four siblings living together in a children’s home housing about 30 children. The youngest, just 18 months old, learned to walk with the help of the oldest sibling, aged 12. Investigators concluded that virtually all the rights of the four children had been violated, illustrating the inability of an overwhelmed system to provide adequate care to some of Hungary’s most vulnerable youngsters. CHILDREN WITHOUT HOMES About 2,700 children were either living in inappropriate placements or waiting in dangerous family circumstances because suitable accommodation could not be found, investigators reported. Some children were placed as far as 500 kilometers (310 miles) from their families, while obtaining specialist accommodation could take as long as a year. Others remained in hospitals for weeks or even months because authorities had nowhere suitable to send them. Authorities record about 17,000 runaway incidents annually, with roughly 800 children considered long-term runaways from state care. Institutions often lacked sufficient psychiatric, psychological, and crisis-care capacity to deal with children suffering from severe trauma or behavioral problems, investigators found. State Secretary Szilvia Gyurkó, responsible for children’s rights and child protection, recalled meeting a young girl who had suffered from scabies for a year and whose head had been shaved. She said the case illustrated what she called “service deserts” in Hungary’s child protection system, where children can carry the consequences of inadequate state care on their own bodies. GOVERNMENT PROMISES ACTION Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s government has acknowledged the scale of the crisis and announced a 9.5 billion forint emergency program, worth roughly 27 million euros ($32 million), to improve conditions. Magyar said his government must learn from past mistakes as it attempts to overhaul a system that deteriorated during Orbán’s administration. Gyurkó has spoken emotionally about what officials encountered while examining the system. “In recent weeks, I have cried a lot,” she said while discussing conditions uncovered during the investigation. The government says hundreds of pages of earlier documents show that officials under Orbán already knew about major shortcomings in the system. ORBÁN-ERA INSPECTIONS Among those documents were reports from nationwide inspections ordered after Hungary’s 2024 presidential pardon of a deputy director who enabled child sex abuse at an orphanage. Inspectors examined hundreds of residential child-protection institutions and documented abuse, hunger, deteriorating buildings, staff shortages, and other deficiencies. Yet the detailed inspection reports were only made public after investigative journalists pursued a freedom-of-information lawsuit and won a final appeal in April 2026. The documents were handed over after the change of government in May. Officially, staff vacancies across the system stood at about 16 percent in some assessments, although professionals interviewed for the new investigation described even more severe shortages. By July 31, 97 state-run children’s groups had closed, while one reception home designed for 16 children at one point had 48 assigned to it. Some employees were working around 80 hours of overtime per month as institutions struggled to maintain basic services. SYSTEM NEAR COLLAPSE Professionals told investigators that prevention and early intervention had effectively broken down. One said children sometimes entered state care only “when blood is already flowing.” The government assessment concludes that outright collapse is currently being prevented largely by the dedication and extra work of individual professionals, together with improvised local solutions. However, the findings come at a politically sensitive moment. While Magyar’s government is promising emergency intervention in child protection, former Prime Minister Orbán has been attempting to rebuild his defeated Fidesz party. Addressing senior Fidesz figures as he announced a new political start, Orbán declared: “I am back.” Yet Hungary’s own investigation suggests the child protection crisis will require far more than political declarations. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqwy.text: Image source, Getty Images By Maia Davies Â and Â Sarah Rainsford ,Â Southern and Eastern Europe correspondent Published 15 October 2026, 09:11 BST Updated 1 hour ago Russia has accused Ukraine of attacking an oil refinery after Volodymyr Zelensky said such strikes, halted at the request of the US, would resume. Ukraine's president said he had restricted attacks for three days while Russia had continued striking Ukrainian energy infrastructure. "We're done," he told the Financial Times , external . Zelensky also accused the US of withdrawing intelligence-sharing on Russian strikes to pressure Kyiv into ending attacks altogether after it struck a deal to import Russian diesel, and he said curbs on Starlink satellite services used by Ukraine's military were deliberate. Ukrainian defence sources told the BBC some Starlink functionality had resumed as of Thursday morning. They said its military service Starshield's "operation while on the move" had been restored, although it remains unclear whether the restrictions to the speed at which drones could fly while still maintaining Starlink internet connection have been fully lifted. Officials were still working to clarify "the reasons and circumstances" behind the move, the sources added. In a separate development, seven people are missing after a drone attack set a chemical tanker on fire off Romania , according to naval officials. Moscow said it had hit two cargo ships with military cargo heading to Ukraine's Odesa port, without naming them. Why is Starlink internet so important on the battlefield in Ukraine? Published 4 hours ago Eight crew missing after drone attack leaves tanker ablaze off Romania's coast Published 1 hour ago The Kremlin said Kyiv had "attempted a large-scale attack" on a refinery south of Moscow early on Thursday. According to Russia's defence ministry, four missiles and dozens of drones were intercepted and the falling debris caused a fire at the site in Ryazan. Zelensky said dozens of Ukrainian cities had come under Russian attack in the past day. He previously said he would agree to the "energy ceasefire" announced by US President Donald Trump on Sunday if Moscow also abided by it. But he accused Russia of ignoring the proposed deal within hours of it being announced, with strikes leaving hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians without power. The Kremlin never said it had agreed to the deal. Zelensky agreed that he felt betrayed by the US when asked by Piers Morgan on Wednesday night, after Washington appeared to withdraw key elements of its support. European leaders have rallied around the Ukrainian president. Italy's Defence Minister Guido Crosetto told the BBC that the US restricting its intelligence-sharing with Kyiv would be a "complete mistake". "Because it is a fundamental form of support. This means denying a country any chance of defending itself." He added: "Peace will be achieved when [Russian President Vladimir] Putin will be convinced that there is a stalemate... that he cannot advance anymore. But if he sees a weakness on the Ukrainian front, if the United States takes its resources away, then Putin will think he can win, and so he will continue the war." Zelensky told the FT that Ukrainian officials had been told by US counterparts that "if you will not stop [the strikes], we will block intelligence". Ukraine's military relies on US early-warning alerts of incoming Russian aerial attacks to mount air defences, limiting successful strikes, while Starlink internet links are used throughout its war effort to guide drones and protect its skies. There were suggestions a technical glitch was to blame for the sudden Starlink restrictions on Tuesday evening, but owner Elon Musk appeared to deny this and suggested it was the Trump administration's doing . "It was not a technical problem, it was the will," Zelensky told the FT. Trump has denied halting intelligence-sharing. Starlink's sister service Starshield is provided to Ukraine under a US defence department contract. The BBC has approached the US authorities for comment. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Zelensky has questioned Trump's relationship with Russia President, Vladimir Putin Zelensky spoke to the FT during a visit to London on Wednesday which also included a meeting with Prime Minister Andy Burnham in Downing Street - who announced the UK would speed up delivery of lightweight multirole missiles to Kyiv . The Ukrainian president told the FT he would now only halt strikes on Russian oil infrastructure - which Kyiv says are vital to cutting off revenue streams to its war machine - if the US supplied more Patriot air defence missiles. Ukraine has suffered a shortage of the US-made defences since the outbreak of the Iran war consumed stockpiles. Striking a more defiant tone than recently, the Ukrainian president told the newspaper his American counterpart had an affinity for autocratic leaders like Putin. He said it was not up to him to mend US-Ukrainian relations given the events of the past week: "We didn't destroy any relationship." Tensions have previously frayed between the two leaders. After returning to the White House last year, the pair shared a fiery Oval Office meeting in which Trump implied Zelensky was the main block to a peace deal. Zelensky has since walked a careful diplomatic line, showing willingness towards US-brokered deals while stressing that the terms of any peace deal must be just. But he criticised the agreement between Russia and the US to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel to the US and global marketplace , struck last week, as the US effectively investing in Russia's war effort. That deal was the latest effort by Trump to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of the midterm elections, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war. That conflict has sent the cost of petrol - and in particular diesel - skyrocketing, souring his standing with the American public. Zelensky told the FT: "The question will be: when will the next deal be? Maybe it will be gas. Definitely it will be gas." With Russia continuing to strike Ukraine, Zelensky suggested the disruptions to US support was no coincidence. Why Moscow is staying tight-lipped on Trump's energy ceasefire Published 2 days ago Starlink restrictions in Ukraine war linked to political situation, Zelensky aide says Published 1 day ago Local officials report at least 13 people were killed across Ukraine on Wednesday in what Zelensky called a "constant", large-scale Russian attack. He said more than 850 drones had been launched at dozens of cities and communities. At least three people were killed in the central region of Kirovohrad as it suffered its largest attack since Russia's full-scale invasion began in 2022, officials there said, with nearly 360 drones launched during a 10-hour barrage. Deaths were also reported in Donetsk, Kherson and Volyn. "It is clear that Russia deliberately escalated these attacks, taking advantage of the easing of sanctions and seeing attempts to pressure Ukraine," Zelensky wrote on social media. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crx2.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images By Basillioh Rukanga ,Â Emery Makumeno ,Â BBC Africa ,Â Reporting from Kinshasa Â and Â Makuochi Okafor ,Â BBC Africa ,Â Reporting from Lagos Published 26 October 2026, 08:16 GMT Updated 3 hours ago A nurse has been killed and another health worker seriously injured in an attack as they were responding to an Ebola alert in north-eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. The two were targeted by local youths who accused them of contaminating water sources and spreading the Ebola virus, according to the UN-backed Radio Okapi. The World Health Organization (WHO) condemned the attack. In an attempt to prevent the virus spreading, neighbouring Uganda has banned all non-essential travel to and from DR Congo and says its citizens returning from there will be quarantined for 21 days. More than 4,800 people have died and nearly 10,000 been infected in DR Congo since this outbreak began in May. Reacting to the attack in DR Congo, WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said health workers "must be able to carry out their duties in safety and dignity", adding that healthcare personnel should always be protected. The UN agency also extended its condolences to the family and colleagues of the nurse who was killed and wished the injured worker a swift recovery. The BBC has contacted the Ebola response team for comment on the circumstances surrounding the attack in DR Congo. This is not the first time such an attack has happened in DR Congo. Last month, a politician was beaten to death after promoting measures to stop the spread of Ebola, while in August, the Red Cross said its volunteers had been injured and an ambulance set on fire in 11 violent incidents during the first 100 days after the outbreak was declared. Earlier this month, two countries - Kenya and Nigeria - reported their first cases of Ebola linked to the current outbreak. The patient in Nigeria was on Monday flown from Abuja to Switzerland for further treatment. She is the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat who had travelled to the Ugandan capital for a holiday, according to the head of Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention Jean Kaseya. She was evacuated alongside her husband, who has shown no symptoms. Nigeria's health ministry said she was stable, conscious and able to communicate. Authorities are now trying to establish where she contracted the virus. The new restrictions announced in Uganda come after questions were raised over her case and that of a Kenyan businessman. Both tested positive for Ebola after travelling through Uganda, even though no cases have been reported there since August. The Kenyan had arrived from DR Congo where he had business interests. Only essential travellers, including aid workers, truck drivers and security personnel, will be allowed to cross the border from DR Congo to Uganda, subject to strict health screening, the health ministry announced. In addition, all travellers entering Uganda, regardless of their country of origin, will be required to complete locator forms to facilitate contact tracing where necessary. It said returning Ugandans would "undergo 21 days of quarantine at their own cost". About 60 people who were being monitored after coming into contact with the Kenyan patient have all been discharged, it added. In Kenya , the first group of 20 contacts of the first case have gone home, after spending 21 days in quarantine, the health ministry announced on Monday. Another 98 are still being supervised, while seven people who have tested positive for Ebola were stable it said. The Kenyan businessman died two days after arriving in Nairobi. A second woman, related to the businessman, died over the weekend. 'They said it isn't real': Ebola rumours fuel attacks on health workers Published 9 July Is Ebola under control in Kenya after nine cases confirmed? Published 5 days ago Questions remain over Ebola patient who travelled across three nations undetected Published 10 October "All these are measures to ensure that we keep Uganda free of Ebola," Uganda's Health Minister Chris Baryomunsi told the BBC's Newsday programme. Since the two cases were reported in Kenya and Nigeria this month, Uganda has repeatedly stressed that no cases have been reported within its borders. Uganda recorded 20 Ebola cases and two people died shortly after the outbreak started in DR Congo, but the World Health Organization declared the country free of the disease in August. The two passengers tested positive after passing through Uganda's Entebbe airport on the same day. Diana Atwine, the health ministry's permanent secretary, said CCTV camera footage showed no physical interaction between the two patients. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Health Minister Chris Baryomunsi said the measures were meant to keep the country free of Ebola Ugandan officials had previously said the patient in Nigeria had travelled to eastern DR Congo, only transiting through Uganda. On Sunday, however, the health ministry said Uganda and Nigeria were both working to establish her movements, complete travel history and possible routes of exposure. The Ugandan health minister said the recent cases meant the risk had not ended and further underscored the need to "remain vigilant". "We share a border with [DR Congo], where transmission continues, and our communities remain closely connected through trade, travel and family ties," Baryomunsi said. The disease spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit. The Bundibugyo species of Ebola behind this outbreak is relatively rare and there is still no vaccine or specific treatment - though trials are under way. https://telex.hu/kulfold/2026/11/09/megh.text: Hétfőn kora reggel meghalt a kórházban a 24 éves Michał Oksiński, aki szombaton tüzet nyitott Krakkó főterén, számolt be hétfőn a lengyel rendőrség. Mint megírtuk , szombat délután egy katonai jellegű ruházatot viselő fegyveres autójából lövöldözni kezdett Krakkó belvárosában. Hat ember meghalt, a támadót is számba véve összesen 16-an sérültek meg. Az elkövető a családtagjait is megölhette : szülei és a húga holttestét 200 kilométerre Krakkótól, a lakásában találták meg. A férfit a lengyel sajtó a 24 éves Michał Oksińskiként azonosította, a fiatalember legálisan tarthatott fegyvert otthon. Marcin Kierwinski lengyel belügyminiszter korábbi közlése szerint minden jel arra utal, hogy a férfi a szélsőjobboldali ideológiák megszállottja volt. A támadót egy közvetlen tűzharcban ártalmatlanította két fiatal rendőr – bár Oksiński is túlélte a tűzharcot, mostanáig kritikus állapotban kezelték a kórházban. A krakkói ügyészség terrorcselekmény és sorozatgyilkosság ügyében indított nyomozást. Eryk Stasielak, a lengyel államügyészség munkatársa hétfőn közölte a PAP hírügynökséggel: a merénylő halála nincs befolyással a tervezett ügyészségi eljárásra, amelynek során egyebek mellett a férfi indítékait és esetleges kapcsolatait vizsgálják, írta az MTI. Szombat este a lengyel államfő, Karol Nawrocki kétnapos nemzeti gyászt rendelt el az országban. A támadás helyszínét vasárnap estére megnyitották, és misét mutattak be a város főtemplomában az elhunytak tiszteletére. Łukasz Gibała krakkói polgármester kezdeményezésére hétfő este néma menetet tartanak az áldozatok tiszteletére a város főterén, ahol a lövöldözés kezdődött. Az egész Lengyelországot sokkoló lövöldözésről ebben a cikkben írtunk bővebben .
